title: Small but mighty!
date: Reviewed in the United States on May 20, 2026
review: I purchased a much more expensive bug zapper and I’m glad I returned it and got this one. It’s much cheaper and yet the cord is short, but there are always extension cords. It works great I hear zapping all the time and it’s super easy to clean and it’s cute small not bulky and it catches just as many flies and mosquitoes. I’m so happy with this product. I’m thinking of getting a couple more for different parts of the house.

title: So far has worked great!
date: Reviewed in the United States on April 22, 2026
review: I have used this twice so far and it has worked absolutely beautifully! I love that it is a plugin, You can change the light bulb when needed, it is lightweight. My only role complaint so far is that it is so lightweight that I'm a little worried that it'll get knocked over in a strong wind. So I'm going to attempt to weigh it down as you can open the bottom. I'm thinking maybe getting some of those decorative rocks that you can get at the dollar store and using some hot glue. Just to give it some weight so it doesn't blow over in the wind.

title: Long Lasting Bulb!
date: Reviewed in the United States on March 29, 2026
review: I've had this since May 2024 and I've used it every day since (sometimes let it run overnight) and the bulb just now ran out on 03/29/2026.  Since I live in Texas and unfortunately in an apartment where neighbors constantly go in and out I have to deal with a constant supply of fresh gnats coming through the vents. They drive me insane and I LOVE hearing that zap.  I bought another brand and put in another room and I never hear that zap which is very disappointing since I'm unsure it works.  They look similar but this one seems to work better.

title: Kills flying gnats ha ha ha YES!!!
date: Reviewed in the United States on August 30, 2024
review: What I like most is the clean snap that I can hear when a gnat, lured in by the black light tries to land on the bulb, but gets cooked by the spark passing through it to reach the second grid. That's one sweet sound, after trying cider vinegar and water with a drop of dish soap in it. The liquid works great for fruit flies, and these appear to be such at first glance, but they are not and are not attracted to the things fruit flies are. The gnats are tiny, like the light produced from a phone screen, follow the reflected phone light to the face of the person using the phone, then the warm air exiting from the nose, and the next breath in, sucks a gnat into your nose, and that's not pleasant at all. I have been bothered all winter by gnats. To tiny for fly swaters, and sprays, to quick for hands, I thought about using hanging flying insect killer strips until it said that it should be in a room that people occupy less than 4 hours a day. That's not what I consider safe for inside. I have had a 2 bulb, rectangular bug zapper that died after years of faithful service. Thinking that the bulbs would be the shortest life of the thing, I ordered a good supply of extras. I still have bulbs, but the zapper is no longer available sadly. I thought that this might serve as a replacement zapper, although it uses horse shoe shaped bulb of the same wattage, but only a single bulb instead of two.Well I got it unpacked and plugged in and in short order I was able to hear that snap of success,  as "Another One Bites The Dust"!! The unit has a cleaning brush to tidy the grids, but I expect to just use a small cordless vacuum cleaner to remove any debris that is found in the grid or bottom of the zapper. I will check for a source of bulb replacements after 30 days, since I will know by then if I will keep it. So far however I am thrilled that I am reducing the number of flying pests that I have been trying to remove since last season. Sometimes it makes two snaps in succession, a double whammy!!!! Like a home run with the bases loaded!!! Buy it, it works inside without any toxic chemicals, safe around pets and children too. Unless you have flies for pets, lol.

title: An Ostentatious Violet Menace to the Local Commute
date: Reviewed in the United States on April 21, 2026
review: As someone who prides themselves on a 360-degree perspective of the neighborhood, I find the Dickinda 4200V to be an absolute affront to civil liberties. From a purely architectural standpoint, the grid design is suspiciously welcoming—almost flirtatious—which feels like a trap for those of us who appreciate a well-ventilated patio.The primary issue is the light. It is a garish, ultraviolet siren song that is frankly impossible to ignore during one’s evening reconnaissance. It’s "high-powered" in the same way a sledgehammer is high-powered for cracking a peppercorn. 4200 volts? In this economy? It’s excessive. It creates a percussive "pop" that is not only a noise pollutant but serves as a grim reminder that several of my most talented associates—individuals who could walk on ceilings with unparalleled grace—have "retired" suddenly after seeking a closer look at the violet glow.Furthermore, the waterproof casing is a cynical touch. It ensures that even during a refreshing drizzle, there is no sanctuary for those of us just looking for a modest sugar cube or a damp trash lid to call home. It’s far too efficient at "clearing the air," which, if you ask me, makes for a very lonely backyard experience.If you value the delicate, rhythmic humming of the local ecosystem (or just want to avoid the smell of "charred ambition" near your grill), I suggest you stick to something less aggressive. A nice, sticky strip of yellow tape is much more vintage—and at least it gives a fellow a chance to think about his life choices before the end.One star. I’d give it zero, but my hands are currently occupied rubbing themselves together in existential dread.
